book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook defines stagflation first and then lists its causes. Here the video first builds the normal rule (GDP up, unemployment down, inflation up, and the reverse) as a long cause chain, fixes it in a three-column direction table, ties it to the Phillips curve already taught, and only then introduces stagflation as a 'twist in the story' that breaks one cell of the table. The 'how can this be?' question is answered with a different cause chain (oil prices) on the same economy diagram, so the exception is understood against the rule.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Build the normal cause chain and freeze it as a direction table; then teach the new term as the one row that breaks the table, and explain that row with a second cause chain on the same diagram.

talmel_summary: Most of the picture is words: text chains and a direction table whose cells fill as the voice says each direction, so the picture often repeats the speech. It works when structure carries the meaning: the red stagflation row under two green normal rows shows the broken pattern at a glance, the STAG|FLATION split shows the word's parts, and the oil shock is worked through the same economy flow. Weak spots: a long sentence box lands 10-20 s before the voice reaches it, and the 1970s date is only on screen while the voice says 'suppose'.

voice.notes: About 173 words per minute, calm and steady. Long chains are spoken as 'aur agar... to...' links, each step a short clause. The twist is marked by wording ('kahani mein ek twist hai') more than by a pause. Directions are said in English (increase, decrease) inside Hindi sentences, matching the table words. Speech recognition lost about 11 s around 213-224 s, so that stretch is not described here.

game_ideas.player_does: For each scenario card (boom, slump, oil shock), sets an up or down arrow under GDP, inflation and unemployment before the system plays it.
game_ideas.process_happens: The economy flow runs the scenario: factories hire or fire, wages and prices move, and the table row fills with the real directions.
game_ideas.win: All three arrows right for every scenario.
game_ideas.lose: Using the normal rule on the oil shock (inflation down because GDP is down) turns the row red with a big '?', and the oil barrel's cost band on raw material shows why prices rose anyway.

game_ideas.player_does: Builds the oil-shock chain by dragging cards onto the economy flow: oil price up, raw-material cost up, production cost up, prices up, demand down, growth slows, GDP down, unemployment up.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each placed card lights its node on the flow and the meter it touches moves (price meter up, GDP meter down).
game_ideas.win: The finished chain ends with both the price meter up and the GDP meter down: the STAGFLATION tag lights.
game_ideas.lose: A card in the wrong place makes a meter move the wrong way, and the narrator line explains which link was skipped.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a factory in a growing economy and decides wages each quarter to keep and attract workers while rivals bid for the same staff.
game_ideas.process_happens: Higher wages raise unit cost; the player chooses whether to raise shelf prices; the town's price level and unemployment meters update.
game_ideas.win: Stay staffed and profitable through the boom.
game_ideas.lose: Keeping wages low loses workers to rivals; raising them without raising prices wipes out profit, showing why boom wages end up as inflation.
game_ideas.concept: GDP growth -> low unemployment -> wage-cost inflation

checks_learned: A sentence box should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice reaches its content (here a wages box led by 10-20 s).
If the voice frames an example as hypothetical ('maan lijiye'), the screen must not add a real date the voice never says; either both say it or neither.
Every cause chain the narration finishes ('yaani inflation rise karega') must end in a drawn node for that last step.
An exception must be drawn in the same table or diagram as the rule it breaks (the red row under the green rows worked; enforce it).
After a question to the viewer, the answer must return to the same cell that held the '?' and replace it.
A term written on screen must be spelled the same in every video of the series (PHILIPS vs Phillips).

teaching_best.why: The rule is built first, so stagflation lands as a surprise twist: one red row breaking two green ones.
The word is split into STAG and FLATION, each half tied to its meaning: an easy memory hook.
The oil shock runs on the same resources -> economy -> GDP flow used at the start, so the cause sits where the learner already looks.
Running the scenario in reverse fills the second table row without a new explanation.

teaching_weak.why: About 70 s of a text-only cause chain before any picture changes meaningfully; the profit step is spoken but never drawn.
The Phillips curve claim and the GDP-inflation link are restated over a nearly unchanged frame for about 40 s.
A wages sentence box appears long before the voice gets there, so the learner reads ahead and stops listening.
The closing line only says 'these were the details'; the cause (cost push) is not recapped.
